title: EAGER vs LAZY? Default fetch per association? Lazy loading internals (proxy, on-demand SQL)? Hibernate.initialize()? LazyInitializationException in prod? Eager/lazy in plain Java? load() vs get()? getReference/getById vs findById?
shortTitle: What is EAGER vs LAZY fetching?

s1_definition.profdef: `LAZY` (default for `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToMany`): collection loaded ONLY when accessed. Hibernate creates a proxy that triggers SQL on first method call. `EAGER` (default for `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne`): loaded immediately with parent — causes N+1 if not careful. **Always override to LAZY.** `LazyInitializationException`: accessing a lazy collection after the session/TX closes. Fix: fetch inside TX (JOIN FETCH/EntityGraph), NOT re-enable OSIV. `Hibernate.initialize(entity.getCollection())`: forces a lazy load within active session. `getReference()`/`getById()`: returns a LAZY PROXY without DB hit — cheap for FK setting. `findById()`: hits DB immediately, returns `Optional`.
s1_definition.analogy: LAZY = the vault clerk only fetches a customer's transactions when you ASK for them. EAGER = the clerk fetches ALL transactions every time you mention the customer name — even if you only wanted the name. LazyInitializationException = you asked for transactions AFTER the vault was already closed for the night.
s1_definition.oneliner: Always LAZY. Override @ManyToOne to LAZY. Fetch inside TX. Never OSIV. getReference = proxy (no DB). findById = immediate DB hit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `LAZY` (default for `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToMany`): collection loaded ONLY when accessed. Hibernate creates a proxy that triggers SQL on first method call. `EAGER` (default for `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToOne`): loaded immediately with parent — causes N+1 if not careful. **Always override to LAZY.** `LazyInitializationException`: accessing a lazy collection after the session/TX closes. Fix: fetch inside TX (JOIN FETCH/EntityGraph), NOT re-enable OSIV. `Hibernate.initialize(entity.getCollection())`: forces a lazy load within active session. `getReference()`/`getById()`: returns a LAZY PROXY without DB hit — cheap for FK setting. `findById()`: hits DB immediately, returns `Optional`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** LAZY = the vault clerk only fetches a customer's transactions when you ASK for them. EAGER = the clerk fetches ALL transactions every time you mention the customer name — even if you only wanted the name. LazyInitializationException = you asked for transactions AFTER the vault was already closed for the night.

**One line to remember:** Always LAZY. Override @ManyToOne to LAZY. Fetch inside TX. Never OSIV. getReference = proxy (no DB). findById = immediate DB hit.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me set the scene with a real problem that bit our team at National Bank of India. Our trade API worked perfectly on every developer's laptop and sailed through QA. The moment it hit production, it started throwing `LazyInitializationException` on the exact same endpoint. Nothing in the code had changed. Developers were confused and a little scared, because "works on my machine but not in prod" is the worst kind of bug.

Problem 1 — the hidden safety net that only exists locally. In Spring Boot, `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true` is ON by default, and it keeps the Hibernate session open all the way through the controller's response — including JSON serialization. On local machines nobody had turned it off, so when the JSON serializer touched a lazy `trades` collection, the session was still quietly open and it worked. In production the platform team had set `open-in-view=false` for performance (an open-in-view session holds a database connection for the entire request, which starves the connection pool under load). With that net removed, the serializer touched the lazy collection AFTER the `@Transactional` service method had already returned and closed the session — and it blew up. This is exactly how LazyInitializationException works: a lazy proxy firing SQL with no session behind it.

Problem 2 — loading data we never send back. Even when it "worked" locally, the endpoint was eagerly pulling full `Account` rows for trades that only displayed a symbol and amount. That is wasted database work and the root of N+1. This is exactly where a DTO projection helps — we fetch ONLY the fields we return, inside the transaction, so no lazy proxy ever escapes to the serializer.

Problem 3 — creating a trade without wastefully loading the account. When a customer places a trade we only need to stamp the `account_id` foreign key. Loading Rajesh's entire account row (name, balance, status) just to set an FK is pure waste. This is exactly where `getReference` shines: it gives us a proxy carrying just the id, so Hibernate writes the FK with zero extra SELECTs.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `Trade` entity with a `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)` association to `Account`, overriding the dangerous EAGER default. There is a `TradeDTO` holding only `tradeId`, `symbol`, and `amount` — no account fields. The `TradeRepository` has a `findByAccountId` finder. The `TradeService` is annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for reads: it loads trades and maps each one to a `TradeDTO` inside the transaction, so the session is still open during mapping and nothing lazy leaks out. A second service method, `createTrade`, uses `em.getReference(Account.class, accountId)` to set the FK without loading the full account, then persists. The `TradeController` returns `List<TradeDTO>`, which is plain data with no proxies, so JSON serialization is completely safe even with open-in-view disabled. The demo will show the broken path (entity serialized outside TX throws), then the fixed DTO path, and finally the efficient getReference-based create.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a request to list all trades for Rajesh's savings account `SAV2001`, followed later by a request to create a new trade on the same account.

Step 1: The read begins. A service method annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` calls `tradeRepo.findByAccountId("SAV2001")`. The transaction is now open, so a Hibernate session is active and will stay active for the whole method.

Step 2: Hibernate loads the `Trade` entities for that account. But here is the original trap — each `Trade` has a `@ManyToOne Account`, and the default for `@ManyToOne` is EAGER. So for every distinct account referenced, Hibernate fires a SEPARATE `SELECT` against the accounts table. With many trades this becomes the N+1 problem: one query for the trades plus N queries for the accounts.

Step 3: The fix is applied at the mapping. We annotate the association `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)`. Now the `Account` on each trade is just a lightweight proxy — no account SQL fires during the load. The data for the account is not fetched because nothing has touched it yet.

Step 4: The service maps each `Trade` into a `TradeDTO` carrying ONLY `tradeId`, `symbol`, and `amount`. Because we never call `trade.getAccount()`, the lazy proxy is never triggered and no extra query runs. This mapping happens while the transaction is still open. When the `@Transactional` method returns, the session closes — but all the data we need is already sitting safely inside plain DTOs.

Step 5: The controller returns `List<TradeDTO>`. During JSON serialization there is NO LazyInitializationException, because a DTO is plain data with no lazy proxies attached — there is nothing left for the serializer to accidentally trigger. This works identically whether open-in-view is on or off.

Step 6: Now the create path. To create a trade for `SAV2001` we call `em.getReference(Account.class, "SAV2001")`, which returns a proxy carrying just the id and fires NO SELECT. We call `trade.setAccount(proxy)` and then `em.persist(trade)`. On flush, Hibernate writes `INSERT INTO trades (..., account_id) VALUES (..., 'SAV2001')` — the foreign key is set correctly and the full Account row was never loaded from the database.

```
2026-10-17 21:44:07 INFO  TradeService - [READ] findByAccountId("SAV2001") inside @Transactional(readOnly=true)
2026-10-17 21:44:07 FINE  TradeService - Account association is LAZY proxy — no account SELECT fired
2026-10-17 21:44:07 INFO  TradeService - Mapped 3 Trade → TradeDTO [tradeId, symbol, amount] inside TX
2026-10-17 21:44:07 INFO  TradeController - Returned List<TradeDTO> — JSON serialized with NO LazyInitializationException
2026-10-17 21:44:07 INFO  TradeService - [CREATE] em.getReference(Account, "SAV2001") → proxy, 0 SELECT
2026-10-17 21:44:07 INFO  TradeService - persist(trade) → INSERT trades(..., account_id='SAV2001') — Account never loaded
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ FETCH TYPE DEFAULTS ═══

  @ManyToOne, @OneToOne  → default EAGER (loaded with parent) ← OVERRIDE TO LAZY!
  @OneToMany, @ManyToMany → default LAZY (loaded on access)  ← keep LAZY

  ═══ LAZY LOADING INTERNALS ═══

  dematRepo.findById("DEM-001"):
    → SQL: SELECT * FROM demat_accounts WHERE demat_id='DEM-001'
    → holdings field: Hibernate creates PersistentBag PROXY (not loaded)
    → proxy stores the query but does NOT execute it yet

  demat.getHoldings().size():  (within active TX)
    → proxy triggers: SELECT * FROM stock_holdings WHERE demat_id='DEM-001'
    → holdings loaded into memory
    → subsequent calls use the cached collection (first-level cache)

  demat.getHoldings().size():  (OUTSIDE TX — session closed)
    → LazyInitializationException! Session is closed. Cannot load.

  ═══ getReference vs findById ═══

  findById("DEM-001"):
    → SQL: SELECT * FROM demat_accounts WHERE demat_id='DEM-001'
    → Returns: full entity object (all fields populated)
    → Use when: you need to READ entity data

  getReference("DEM-001") / getById("DEM-001"):
    → NO SQL! Returns: LAZY PROXY with only ID set
    → Accessing other fields later → triggers SELECT
    → Use when: setting FK without loading parent
    → Example: holding.setDematAccount(getReference("DEM-001"))
      → INSERT INTO stock_holdings (demat_id='DEM-001') — no SELECT on demat_accounts!

  ═══ LazyInitializationException FIXES ═══

  BAD: return entity from service → controller accesses lazy collection → EXCEPTION
  BAD: spring.jpa.open-in-view=true (session open during view rendering — anti-pattern)

  GOOD: JOIN FETCH in repository query (1 query, all data loaded inside TX)
  GOOD: @EntityGraph on repository method (declarative fetch plan)
  GOOD: Hibernate.initialize() within TX (extra query — less efficient than JOIN FETCH)
  GOOD: Map to DTO within @Transactional method (never return entities to controller)
```

```
  ═══ HLD — EAGER vs LAZY Fetching (Banking) ═══

  ┌────────────┐ HTTPS ┌──────────────┐ REST ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Mobile App │──────→│ API Gateway  │─────→│ Account Service (×4)   │  ← Application
  └────────────┘       │ JWT          │      │ Spring Boot + JPA      │
                       └──────────────┘      └──────────┬───────────┘
                           LAZY proxy loaded             │ inside open session
                           on first access                ▼
                                      ┌───────────────────────────────┐
                                      │ PostgreSQL                     │  ← Data Layer
                                      │ child rows fetched on demand    │
                                      └───────────┬─────────────────────┘
                                                  │
                                                  ▼

  @ManyToOne/@OneToOne default EAGER; collections default LAZY.
  LAZY returns a proxy; access outside session → LazyInitializationException.
  Hibernate.initialize()/JOIN FETCH load within TX; getReference = lazy proxy.
  Observability: LazyInitException rate, fetch-plan audits. Security: unchanged.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Fetch Strategy & Proxies (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Lazy Proxy: Hibernate subclass defers DB load until access       │
  │  Virtual Proxy: getReference returns proxy without SELECT         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: entity declares associations; query decides what to initialize│
  │  O: tune fetch per use case without rewriting the mapping         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ @Entity Account                                 │
  │  @ManyToOne(fetch=LAZY)  @JoinColumn(...)        │
  │  branch : Branch            ← default EAGER→LAZY │
  │  @OneToMany(mappedBy="account",fetch=LAZY)      │
  │  transactions : List<Transaction>  (proxy)      │
  └───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                          │ initialized via
                          ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ AccountService @Transactional                   │
  │  a = repo.findById(id)                           │
  │  Hibernate.initialize(a.getTransactions())       │
  │  // or JOIN FETCH in repo query                  │
  │  repo.getReferenceById(id) → lazy proxy, no SQL  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  (Caution) Accessing LAZY after TX closes → LazyInitializationException (NOT fixed by OSIV).
  Rule: default LAZY everywhere; initialize explicitly inside the transaction.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Default fetch types are the most common source of accidental over-fetching: ManyToOne and OneToOne default to EAGER, meaning every query for a child entity also loads the parent — cascading into N+1 queries. Always override to LAZY. LazyInitializationException occurs when a lazy collection is accessed after the session closes. The fix is fetching what you need inside the Transactional method via JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph, and mapping to a DTO before returning — never return entities to the controller.

The getReference method returns a lazy proxy that only holds the entity ID without hitting the database. It is efficient for setting foreign keys: `holding.setDematAccount(em.getReference(DematAccount.class, dematId))` generates an INSERT with the FK but no SELECT on the parent table. In contrast, findById immediately executes a SELECT and returns the full entity. Hibernate.initialize forces a lazy collection to load within an active session, but it fires a separate query and does not solve N+1 — JOIN FETCH is always the better approach. Disable OSIV (open-in-view=false) to force proper fetching inside transactions rather than relying on the session being open during view rendering.

### 9.5-9.7 Entity lifecycle, persist/merge, auditing, locking, pagination (Q16-Q22 of 69)

keyPoints: LAZY (default for collections): load on first access — risk LazyInitializationException
EAGER (default for @ManyToOne): load immediately with parent — N+1 risk
Fix LazyInit: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or Hibernate.initialize()
Rule: default to LAZY, use JOIN FETCH when you need the data
